query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted heat‐treatment that promotes the in situ precipitation of a fine, coherent intermetallic phase (e.g., Ni3Ti-like) within the titanium–nickel primary high‐entropy alloy will enhance its elevated‐temperature strength and creep resistance relative to the as‐cast (untreated) alloy by refining the microstructure through controlled precipitate formation.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy composed primarily of titanium and nickel (with each element in the 5–35 at% range, with additional HEA-qualifying minor elements as needed) produced by standard casting or rapid solidification, resulting in a predominantly single solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled aging heat treatment at a moderately high temperature using an inert or vacuum atmosphere, designed to initiate controlled nucleation of a nanoscale intermetallic phase.
generation.conditions: The heat treatment is applied under a protective atmosphere at an elevated aging temperature for an optimized duration to form fine, coherent precipitates without causing excessive coarsening; performance is evaluated under elevated-temperature conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform dispersion of fine, coherent secondary phase precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti-like intermetallic) within the high-entropy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion, providing precipitation strengthening through particle pinning that impedes creep deformation and enhances yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will exhibit a significantly higher yield strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures relative to the as-cast state, owing to the precipitation-induced strengthening.
generation.baseline: The as-cast titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy, which shows a single-phase solid-solution microstructure without refined secondary precipitates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to HEAs that conform to the 5–35 at% per element definition and are designed with titanium and nickel as primary constituents. The beneficial effect is expected within an elevated temperature range up to about 800–1000 °C; it may not hold if the operating temperature or aging parameters lead to precipitate coarsening or phase instability.
generation.uncertainty: Exact heat-treatment parameters (time, temperature) and the thermodynamic stability of the precipitates under prolonged service conditions require further optimization. The precise magnitude of property improvements is uncertain until experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples with identical titanium–nickel primary compositions that meet the HEA definition. Subject one set to the proposed aging heat treatment (e.g., 750 °C for 4 hours in an inert atmosphere) while leaving the second set as-cast. Conduct elevated-temperature mechanical tests (such as tensile tests at 800 °C and creep tests) and microstructural analyses (using TEM and XRD) on both sets.
measurements: Creep rate under a defined stress at elevated temperature
Precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction as determined by TEM/XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant increase (beyond experimental uncertainty) in yield strength and/or a lower creep rate compared to the as-cast samples, or if no coherent precipitates are observed in the microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have gained considerable attention due to their innovative design and outstanding mechanical properties []. HEAs consist of 5~35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, resulting in high configurational entropy, significant lattice distortion, and reduced diffusion rates []. HEAs are typically characterized by configurational entropies exceeding 1.5R (where R is the gas constant) []. The configurational entropy equation is shown in Equation (1). where Δsmix is the constituent entropy, N is the number of elements, and xi is the entropy of each element. Due to their high entropy, HEAs tend to form single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. This unique composition and microstructure give HEAs exceptional mechanical properties. HEAs generally exhibit a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structure []. Unlike typical alloys, HEAs form a concentrated solid solution. Consequently, HEAs exhibit high strength and hardness at room temperature, along with excellent mechanical performance at both low and high temperatures [].

One of the most intensely investigated HEA systems, primarily forming cubic phases is AlCoCrCuFeNi [,]. Due to the positive enthalpy of mixing ∆Hmix among Cu and the elements Fe and Cr, segregation was observed, deteriorating mechanical and corrosion properties. Therefore, subsequent investigations focused on the copper-free derivative AlCoCrFeNi [,,,,]. Early studies concentrated on the equimolar composition. However, investigations showed that optimum properties are usually achieved when choosing a differing chemical composition []. Investigating the influence of different alloying elements showed a strong influence of aluminium on the microstructure, phase composition, and properties [,]. For a low aluminium content, fcc phases are stabilised, whereas high contents of aluminium act as a strong bcc phase stabiliser [,]. In addition, the formation of complex phases can be suppressed for a high aluminium content []. Furthermore, the influence of additional alloying elements has been investigated.
